options.why: Places the beam's weight at the pivot, so it produces no torque.
Torque balance about the pivot gives $mg\,x_p=Mg(L/2-x_p)$.
Ignores the weight of the beam and balances only the hanging object, so the mass must be zero or arbitrary; here uses $M(L/2)/xp$ with the wrong lever arm.
Sets the hanging mass equal to the mass of the beam.

blueprint.concept: Rotational equilibrium of a uniform beam about a pivot

key_conditions.condition: the beam is uniform so its weight acts at the center

must_include: beam, pivot position and hanging object

misconceptions.description: Ignores the weight of the beam and balances only the hanging object, so the mass must be zero or arbitrary; here uses $M(L/2)/xp$ with the wrong lever arm.

Sets the hanging mass equal to the mass of the beam.
Uses the full length as the lever arm of the beam's weight.

verification.independent_path: a bisection root finder on the net torque as a function of the hanging mass recomputes the balancing mass

options.why: Uses $a=mg/I$ with no radius, mixing linear and rotational quantities.

ap_physics_1-m17.stem: The motion diagram shows an object at equal time intervals as it moves along a straight line, with arrows showing the velocity at each position. Which statement describes the acceleration of the object?

stimulus.description: Motion diagram with velocity arrows

options.text: The acceleration cannot be determined without knowing the mass of the object.
options.why: Confuses kinematics, which describes the change in velocity, with dynamics.

options.text: The acceleration is directed to the right.
options.why: Assumes the acceleration always points in the direction of the velocity (or the opposite) without checking whether the speed is increasing or decreasing.

options.text: The acceleration is directed to the left.
options.why: The change in velocity between successive points has this direction, and acceleration points along the change in velocity.

options.text: The acceleration is zero because the object moves in a straight line.
options.why: Treats straight-line motion as unaccelerated even though the spacing between points changes.

key_conditions.evidence: the stem states equal intervals so spacing encodes speed

After the collision the velocities are $-2.00\text{ m/s}$ and $2.00\text{ m/s}$ respectively. Which statement correctly classifies the collision?

stimulus.description: Carts before and after a collision

options.text: The collision cannot be classified without knowing the duration of the contact.
options.why: Believes the time of contact matters for classifying the collision type.

options.text: The collision is elastic, because the total kinetic energy is the same before and after the collision.
options.why: Comparing the total kinetic energy before and after decides the type; momentum is conserved in both types so it cannot distinguish them.

options.text: The collision is perfectly inelastic, because the carts bounce apart at different speeds.
options.why: Mixes up bouncing apart with energy loss, or sticking together with energy conservation.

options.text: The collision is inelastic, because the total momentum is the same before and after the collision.
options.why: Uses conservation of momentum to classify the collision, but momentum is conserved in every isolated collision.
